T01: Elder Gong lays out three doctrinal foundations for temple worship: eternal families, moral agency, and the Holy Spirit of Promise, which makes honored covenants binding. He then describes a "personal temple culture": attending more often as temples come closer, bringing family names, speaking of every temple with gratitude rather than as big or small, and, where possible, owning one's own temple clothes. He tells of members whose hearts softened toward difficult family members through temple work for them.
T02: Sister Runia shares the sudden death of her son Ryan and the lesson she drew from Joseph Smith in Liberty Jail: hard experiences can be for our good. She retires the idea that the gospel is an umbrella that keeps the rain off, describing it instead as the solid rock we stand on in the storm, and teaches that not understanding is not the same as not believing. Her brother's sculpting class illustrates how the Savior, once invited, shapes us into what we could not become alone.
T03: Elder Caussé, recalling the scripture that comforted him at two calls to serve, teaches that bearing witness of Jesus Christ belongs not only to apostles but to every disciple who has taken His name by covenant. A testimony need not be long or eloquent, only true; his niece's two-sentence testimony at camp is his example. He invites everyone to look daily for brief, natural chances to share their witness, linking "I know" and "I love you" as expressions of the same gift.
T04: Elder Sikahema tells of his Tongan grandparents, missionaries who buried their infant son after a storm at sea and still sailed on to hear an apostle in 1947. He traces the ancient famine of hearing the word of the Lord, ended when the Father and the Son appeared to Joseph Smith and prophets and apostles were restored. Opening the conference, he urges listeners not to treat the words of living prophets as a light thing.
T05: Elder Hathaway testifies that Jesus Christ is the great deliverer and that the question for the faithful is not whether He will deliver, but how and when. Drawing on a highway accident at the start of his mission leadership and a missionary who lost her father a week before returning home, he outlines a pattern: opposition raises hard questions, sincere seeking brings assurance, grace enables us to endure, and deliverance comes in the Savior's time and way, some now, some after waiting, and some in the Resurrection.
T06: Elder Soares invites members to live the law of the fast "in a higher and holier way," drawing on Isaiah 58's promises that our light will break forth and the Lord will answer, "Here I am." Joined with earnest prayer, fasting humbles us, aligns our desires with God's will, and invites revelation, following the Savior's own 40-day fast. Fast offerings turn the fast outward to bless those in need, and he promises miracles and greater sensitivity to others to those who embrace it.
T07: Bishop Douglas thanks missionaries of every age and urges the rising generation to place full-time missionary service high on their list. He tells of Elder Merlin Sanchez in Peru, who returned to church at 25 with the help of friends, served faithfully, and now leads a family and a stake. He restates that worthy, able young men are asked to prepare and serve, that a mission is a powerful option for young women to pray about, and that there is still room for everyone.
T08: President Christofferson takes up a subject he calls a duty to address: gambling. He describes how smartphones have turned it into a constant, private activity, cites survey figures showing especially heavy participation among teenage boys and young adults, and explains that the industry's revenue is gamblers' losses. Quoting President Oaks's question "Where will this lead?" and Paul's warning about becoming a stumbling block, he calls gambling morally wrong because it takes without giving, and pleads with members to refrain and use the time and money for good.
T09: Elder Renlund recalls a heart-transplant patient who, days after a near-miraculous recovery, complained that his oatmeal was cold. He likens this to ancient Israel and to us: losing sight of God's past mercies and promises when daily problems loom. Our hope rests on Christ's righteousness, not our own, and he tells of his sister Linda, who learned there is no asterisk excluding her from God's promises, urging listeners to erase their own.
T10: President Farnes recalls a discouraging day as a young priesthood leader when then-Elder Dallin H. Oaks noticed him in the temple, listened, and lifted him. Years later President Oaks did not remember it, but replied that "it's what we do." Linking the sacrament covenant to daily ministering, and telling of helping a frightened new missionary through his first flight, he invites listeners to pray each day for eyes to see the "divine appointments" God places in their path.
T11: Elder Chigbundu, recalling the talk of "immunity" during the COVID-19 pandemic, describes building spiritual immunity through four small and simple things: scripture study, prayer, the sacrament, and keeping covenants, including temple worship. He tells of a homesick new missionary steadied by studying the Book of Mormon and a sister with cancer who felt the Savior's love through daily prayer. These practices, he teaches, are the armor of God that helps us withstand life's challenges.
T12: Elder Giuffra recounts teaching a poor, elderly woman in Chile who believed she could never pay tithing, and his mission president's counsel that there are no exceptions to the law. After she prayed for help, she was baptized and faithfully paid tithing and fast offerings. He testifies that tithing is a law of faith: we keep commandments because we love God, trials still come, and the Lord fulfills His promises in His own time, including, as he has seen in Central America, by helping families break cycles of poverty.
T13: Elder Morgan grew up in another church that also believes in the Book of Mormon, where his single mother read it to him daily. As a teenager he secretly attended Latter-day Saint meetings and gained a testimony; years later his wife identified the reason: "It was covenants," made by his Nauvoo ancestors. He teaches that covenants are generational and have no time limit, and assures parents of wandering children that no one has traveled beyond the reach of God's love.
T14: Elder Fale teaches that every person is a beloved child of heavenly parents, illustrating God's unearned love by showing his children their baby pictures: they did nothing to earn their parents' love and can do nothing to lose it. He warns against the lie that God's love means we will be saved regardless of sin, since exaltation comes through receiving Christ by covenant. Understanding God's love, he says, helps us understand Christ, see past the world's labels, and reject the idea that it is ever too late to change.
T15: Elder Kearon draws on learning to fly gliders as a teenager: pilots seek rising air called "lift" and turn decisively away from sinking air, and without climbing, a glider slowly descends. Spiritual lift and sink are likewise unseen but can be felt, and neglecting spiritual practices can let us sink almost imperceptibly. His counsel is simple: find a faithful guide, tune in to the Spirit, join others who are climbing, turn away from sink, and help others rise, because Jesus Christ loves to lift.
T16: Elder Dunn recalls a 100-mile ultramarathon in which, at mile 90, he wanted to quit until his running partner Ted promised to get him to the finish. A photo later revealed that Ted had quietly carried Elder Dunn's water and pack for those last miles. He likens Ted to the Savior, who rescues not by shortening our course but by helping us lengthen our stride, and promises that feeling broken does not mean God has abandoned us.
T17: Elder Eyring speaks to the moments when we realize "I can't fix this," the thought that came to a friend whose son had died. He shares how he and his wife, who lost one of their twins before birth, comforted a young couple facing the same loss. Self-reliance eventually meets burdens no one can carry alone, and the Savior, who knows our feelings, comforts us especially through the Holy Ghost. Quoting President Oaks on the literal, universal resurrection, he urges listeners to make the constant companionship of the Holy Ghost one of their highest priorities.
T18: Elder Rasband speaks to everyone grieving for loved ones who have turned away from the Lord, acknowledging that lecturing and pressure often widen the rift. He asks them to turn their despair over to Jesus Christ, who loves the wanderer even more and has already paid for their choices, and to lead with love, as Alma's father did in praying for his son. His three suggestions: let go of guilt and never give up, never let a problem matter more than a person, and remember that Christ is the answer.
T19: President Eyring testifies that the promises in the hymn "How Firm a Foundation" are true: the Lord does not remove our trials, but He is with us in them. His mother, who taught him that life is meant to be a test, endured lifelong illness with faith, while his father cared for her and thanked every nurse who helped. Quoting President Kimball that God usually meets our needs through another person, he thanks those who pray for and reach out to others, encourage missionaries, and sustain leaders, and invites more to join them.
T20: President Chibota shares a Southern African greeting meaning "I see you," an acknowledgment that another person matters. The Savior saw individuals where others saw labels, and her daughter's friendship with a school janitor shows how seeing someone can begin with learning their name. She invites listeners this week to learn the name of someone who may feel unseen, to pray to see others as God does, and to replace worldly labels with eternal truths: child of God, child of the covenant, disciple of Jesus Christ.
T21: Elder Andersen welcomes President Rosemary Chibota, who joined the Church at 17 after reading a pamphlet about Joseph Smith, and teaches that spiritual courage, born of faith in Jesus Christ, has always been required of disciples, from Moroni to today. Contrasting his quiet boyhood days herding cows with the constant noise of phones and "artificial information," he urges stillness to nourish faith. Examples range from a young President Oaks accepting a demanding calling to Spokane fire survivors who said their faith was secure, and he promises that strengthening faith brings answers and increased spiritual power.
T22: Elder Fantone recalls signing his own name on his daughter's school form, then fixing it by simply adding her first name, and contrasts that quick fix with what it means to take upon us the name of Christ. Taking His name is not adding a badge but a lifelong determination to serve Him, which King Benjamin teaches we do by serving others. His parents, who gave their children's bedrooms to a student and to children needing a safe home, and homesick missionaries who came to love the work, show how service changes the server.
T23: Elder Dube recalls that in 1987 then-Elder Oaks had a "Trespassers will be prosecuted" sign removed from a mission office gate, teaching him that all are invited to come unto Christ. From Moroni he draws three truths: come, deny yourselves of ungodliness, and be perfected in Him, since we come to Christ to be perfected rather than perfecting ourselves first. A brother struggling to quit smoking set a temple sealing date and was sealed two months later, and Elder Dube invites each listener to help one person come unto Christ.
T24: Elder Cook teaches that integrity and virtue sustain disciples on the covenant path, recalling the inscription that inspired young David O. McKay: "Whate'er thou art, act well thy part." He links virtue and happiness, noting the Declaration of Independence's 250th anniversary, and condemns coarse language and online bullying as violating the Savior's teachings. Repentance is part of integrity; a World War II veteran he taught as a young missionary compared forgiveness to stepping onto the soil of home.
T25: Elder Kyungu takes up President Oaks's April 2026 invitation to forgo contention and use the language of peacemakers. Citing Proverbs, the Savior, and Paul, he gives concrete examples of words that wound, such as "you never listen" or "this is all your fault," and words that build peace, such as "I'm sorry," "I forgive you," and "let us start again." He invites listeners to repent of harsh words, fill their hearts with Christ's doctrine, and become instruments of His peace.
T26: Elder Schmeil describes two divine helps for mortality: the Savior and our covenants, through which we are yoked with Christ and our burdens lightened. He emphasizes that we need not be perfect to partake of the sacrament, only willing to take His name, remember Him, and keep His commandments. Drawing on Haggai, where Israel labored much but accomplished little while the temple lay unbuilt, he invites listeners to "consider your ways" and make covenant relationships with God their priority.
T27: President Oaks testifies that this is Christ's Church and that the way through every struggle, including doubt, is to draw closer to Jesus Christ through daily prayer and scripture study, with patience for others and for ourselves. He urges members to keep their commandments and covenants, protected by the sacrament and temple, and teaches that there is no ultimate conflict between scientific and spiritual ways of knowing. Citing the Book of Mormon's witness that God's grace is for all people, he calls on everyone to act on these truths and share them.
T28: President Uchtdorf, recalling his own baptism in a public swimming pool, teaches that baptism is an individual ordinance that also joins us to a covenant people. While the Savior broke down walls between Jews, Samaritans, and Gentiles, Satan works to divide, yet in Christ's Church we are united by love for God and neighbor and by our covenants, not by politics or culture. He points to the sacrament as a weekly fresh start taken together and invites all to "come and see, come and help, and come and belong."
T29: Speaking to young women, Sister Muñoz Spannaus recalls making a list of aspirations as a girl after studying the 13th article of faith, and likens the Lord to a guide who knows our exact location, as her husband did when her GPS failed. She offers seven practices and invites each young woman to choose one: partake of the sacrament humbly, repent daily, study the scriptures, learn about ministering angels, protect your sleep, limit phone use, and seek friends striving to follow the Lord. She closes by inviting them to write their own list of aspirations.
T30: Elder Villanueva tells how his mother, separated and raising eight children, chose to pay a full tithe when the family joined the Church. When a sister's faith in tithing weakened after a promotion never came, he invited her, as he had done himself, to list the significant but subtle blessings tithing brings, which can be easy to overlook. Recalling the widow of Zarephath, he testifies that the Lord opens the windows of heaven in His own way and time.
T31: Elder Bednar, using the image of a damaged passport rejected at a border, teaches that ordinances and covenants are our credentials for returning to God, and that their integrity must be maintained through ongoing faithfulness, ratified over time by the Holy Spirit of Promise. He explains that a temple sealing has both a marriage aspect and a vertical tie to God's eternal family. To a faithful spouse whose partner breaks covenants, his answer is an emphatic no: another person's choices cannot deprive a covenant keeper of any promised blessing.
T32: Elder Lebethoa, whose name means "joy" and whose wife's means "eternal," recalls their first serious argument as newlyweds and how the Savior's words that contention is not of Him showed them the way forward. Whatever our struggles, he testifies, the answer is Jesus Christ, the light of the world. He suggests three ways to receive more of His light: strengthen faith in Christ, study the scriptures daily, especially the Book of Mormon, and practice daily repentance.
T33: Elder Sinclair recalls a Primary boy who buttoned his sleeve to his lapel and got stuck, and the little girl who quietly freed him while he himself felt only irritation, a moment that taught him to be quick to help and slow to judge. He finds the same pattern in the Savior's treatment of the woman at the well, whom He met with dignity and living water rather than shame. Citing President Oaks's call to seek to be holy like the Savior, he invites members to help new members and friends in more Christlike ways.
T34: Speaking especially to Primary children, Elder Stevenson uses Lehi's vision of the tree of life and his own love of fruit to describe three sweet fruits of the gospel: we are children of a loving Heavenly Father, the great plan of happiness through Jesus Christ, and the gift of the Holy Ghost. He tells of a small boy who ran to the stand to sing "I Am a Child of God" after an earthquake, and of a grieving Buddhist priest comforted by learning where his wife's spirit had gone. He invites children to love, share, and invite.
T35: Brother Reid, newly called to the Sunday School General Presidency and once described in a headline as an NFL player, admits wondering whether he is good enough to teach the gospel. He notes that when the Savior called people to teach, He also promised to make them what He needed. Remembering his parents and Primary teachers in American Samoa, who taught beneath a mango tree and loved each child by name, he teaches that to teach like the Savior we must love like Him, and that a 25-minute lesson is an invitation to focus on helping people come to Christ.
T36: Elder Gilbert teaches that it takes courage to stand for truth and even more to stand for truth with love. Expanding on five principles from a devotional he gave with President Oaks, he counsels: avoid overly contentious settings, first find common ground, be a light, hold to truth even while reaching out, and stay anchored in Jesus Christ. He candidly recalls winning an argument with a hurting friend but losing the Spirit, and quotes President Holland that Christ never withheld His love yet never exempted anyone from His commandments.
T37: In his brief closing remarks, President Oaks invites everyone to study and ponder the conference talks prayerfully and to act in faith on the principles they teach. He announces that the Salt Lake Temple will open to the public on April 5, 2027, points to TempleSquare.org and the Temple Square app, and mentions a new video series premiering after the session. He blesses members with peace and testifies that truth and the covenant path are found in the restored Church of Jesus Christ.
